theme: The LORD says to my Lord, Melchizedek and priesthood
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 110. This is the Old Testament psalm quoted most often in the New Testament. Jesus used it in Matthew 22 to ask the Pharisees a question they could not answer. Read it as the portrait of a king who is also a priest.
settingTheScene: Psalm 110 is a short psalm of David, only seven verses. It records a conversation within God: the LORD speaks to David’s Lord. It describes a king who sits at God’s right hand and a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. Today you read it after Psalm 2 and the Transfiguration, and just before Jesus uses it in the temple.
observation: “The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (v. 1).
“The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies!” (v. 2).
“Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (v. 3).
“The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (v. 4).
“The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath” (v. 5).
“He will execute judgment among the nations” (v. 6).
“He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (v. 7).
“He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses; he will shatter chiefs over the wide earth” (v. 6).
interpretation:
The first verse is a puzzle. David, the king, calls someone “my Lord.” The LORD (Yahweh) speaks to this other Lord and invites him to sit at his right hand, the place of highest honor and authority. Who is this? A king calls no one lord except God. Yet this figure is also David’s descendant. In Matthew 22:41-46, Jesus asks the Pharisees exactly this: if the Christ is David’s son, how does David call him Lord? They have no answer. The answer is that the Messiah is both David’s son and David’s Lord, fully human and fully divine.

The psalm describes his reign. He rules from Zion in the midst of his enemies. His people come willingly, “in holy garments,” ready to serve. His enemies become his footstool.

Then verse 4 gives the second puzzle: this king is also a priest forever. In Israel, kings came from Judah and priests from Levi, and the two offices were kept apart. But Melchizedek was both king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham in Genesis 14. The psalm says the Messiah will be a priest like him, not by genealogy, but by God’s oath. And it is an oath God will not change.

Hebrews builds its whole argument on this verse. Jesus is the priest who offered himself once for all, and is now seated at God’s right hand, where he intercedes for us. He is not standing like the Old Testament priests, whose work was never done. He sits because his work is finished.

The psalm ends with the king refreshed and lifting up his head, a picture of victory. After the Transfiguration and before the passion week, this psalm sets the course: the Son will suffer, be raised, and reign.
connection: Matthew 22:41-46 records Jesus’ question about this psalm. Acts 2:33-36 applies it to the ascension. Hebrews 5:5-10, 7:1-28, and 10:11-14 explain Melchizedek and Christ’s priesthood. Genesis 14:18-20 introduces Melchizedek. Romans 8:34: Christ Jesus is at the right hand of God, interceding for us. 1 Corinthians 15:25 says he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. Colossians 3:1.
application:
Remember today that Jesus is seated at the Father’s right hand, in authority, praying for you.

When you feel guilty, remember that your priest is the perfect one who has offered the final sacrifice.

Offer yourself willingly to his service today, as the psalm says his people do.
prayerPrompts: Worship Jesus as David’s son and David’s Lord.
Thank him that he is a priest forever.
Ask him to make his enemies his footstool in your life too.
